utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you as well, Mr. Dondo. I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony is still binding. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document P1147, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, in direct examination yesterday you testified that the document will you see in a moment on your screen was probably drafted by you. Now, when you say that you drafted document, do you mean that you formulated the document yourself, or was it dictated to you by somebody?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was dictated by Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are the contents of this document true? Is this an accurate report?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which particular case this is related to, so I can't give you an answer, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document number P53, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now while the document is being brought on the screen -- yes, you have it here. Now you have given a statement about this document in your statement to the Defence, D1696. And your testimony was that you were the person who wrote this document. Did someone dictate this document to you, or did you formulate it on your own?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak dictated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take you to paragraph 18 of your statement to the Defence. And that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have, Mr. Registrar, D1696.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now this is what you say about that document. You say --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could you go, Mr. Registrar, to page 7 of the English version. That's paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "I can say that I wrote it. We wrote the document as an order which was the idea of our Office for Cooperation because it was important to assist UNCRO. Mr. Cermak signed the document as we sent it. We did the same when Mr. Cermak told us to write a request for the return of the stolen UN vehicles. We also wrote it in the form of an order." Now you say the idea to write this an order was the Office for Cooperation. At the time Mr. Cermak dictated the document to you, did you discuss as to how, in what format the document should go, that it should go as an order or anything else?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss it. This -- it was formulated as an order because we felt that the document was important in the context of the cooperation with the UN. We decided ourselves that it should be formulated as an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "we," whom are you referring to? The --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The liaison officers' department or office.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And didn't Mr. Cermak have anything to say about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you presented the document, when you said Mr. Cermak dictated it to you, and the document at paragraph 4 says: "This order is effective immediately." That last paragraph was also dictated to you by General Cermak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the customary formulation used in orders. He did not dictate that bit. We wrote it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now did you convey this order from General Cermak to the military police and the Knin police station, who passed this document on to the police and the military police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We gave the letter to Mr. Cermak, and he was to forward it on to whomever was supposed to receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you know of any instance where these orders from General Cermak has reached the civilian police or the military police and they have refused to implement those tasks, saying -- on the basis that General Cermak did not have authority to issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the individuals who received such orders completely ignored Mr. Cermak's orders. For this reason, such orders were issued initially once or twice, and then subsequently, they were formulated as letters only, in view of the fact of the units did not honour them, and in view of the fact that Mr. Cermak did not have any powers over these units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber one specific instance where General Cermak issued such an order and where the unit that was -- it was addressed to ignored the order? Give us an example: What the order was; when it was issued; to which unit it was issued.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly what sort of orders these were, but we were supposed to see what the situation was like concerning the Promina repeater on the hill overlooking Knin, where the Serbs used to have their radio stations. Mr. Cermak told us that we could take the liberty to go up there, together with the UN, and see what the situation was like. However, when we approached the area we were denied access by the military, who told us that the permission from Mr. Cermak was not sufficient, that we needed the permission from the commander of the Military District in order to be able to gain access there. We then subsequently obtained the necessary document from Mr. Ademi and went back to the station, which was on a hill overlooking Promina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you approached the units to get access to this repeater, were you carrying a written order from Mr. Cermak addressed to those units, asking them, ordering them to permit you all to enter the repeater?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, apart from that incident, can you refer to any specific instance where General Cermak issued a written order to either the civilian police or the military police and where they dishonoured it, where they refused to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order to return the vehicles that had been appropriated. He issued the order as such; however, when the command of the operations zone issued an order to that effect as well, only then was the order acted upon, though it wasn't really fully followed up on. And I'm talking about the vehicles that had been appropriated during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What you're referring to is your statement given in D1696, paragraph 24; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could move to paragraph 24 on this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where you say: "I can isolate an example of the return of the stolen UN vehicles when Mr. Cermak sent an order to the civil and military police to find the stolen vehicles and return them to the UN. Mr. Cermak was not superior to the civil and military police. Therefore his order did not cause an effect. After that, Mr. Cermak sent a report to the Chief of Staff of the Split MD and asked him for assistance." Now --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, in the course of your work, did you have the opportunity to get to know the military police officers and civilian police officers operating in the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know the commander of the Knin military police, Mr. -- have you heard of Mr. Bosko Dzolic?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, he testified in these proceedings - and I'm referring to P875, paragraph 44 and P876, paragraph 17 - and let me tell what you he said about the recovery of stolen vehicles. I'll read his testimony to you: "The first time that I attended a meeting with General Cermak was on 8th of August, 1995, when I think two trucks of the International Red Cross had gone missing. There was only Cermak and me at the meeting, and he told me that he had been informed by the International Red Cross that the trucks had been stolen by the Croatian military. I informed the military crime police, and some eight hours later, the trucks were found in the possession of an artillery unit of the 4th Guards Brigade and the trucks were subsequently returned." Did you know about that incident, where General Cermak instructed Mr. Dzolic to find these trucks and the trucks were subsequently returned?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So do you agree with me that there are examples of the military police carrying out General Cermak's request, instructions or orders to recover missing items that you're not aware of?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... hang on. Look, we must not misrepresent evidence to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. -- Ms. Mahindaratne, the issue is orders or no orders. If you then line them up, all three of them, and say that there are examples of, that is like saying if the issue is whether a car is black or white, and then you show -- you show the witness a car of a -- well, a colour which you say, Well, isn't this an example that cars do exist of the colours white, grey, or black. That is, of course, an answer that -- the issue is whether orders were ignored. And in your last question, you said, So you do agree with me that there are examples of the military police carrying out General Cermak's requests, instructions or orders. Now, the whole issue is orders or requests, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. My point was actually - perhaps I did not phrase it properly - that in the given instance -- let me -- let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do remind my learned friend of the evidence of the witness, transcript page 9028, and it's important that if testimony is being used of other people that it is put accurately, in my submission. Otherwise, it may mislead a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I also point out that the same witness, at transcript page 8953, has in fact provided clear testimony on which would have an impact on the issue before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would formulate the matter in such a way, because what usually happens, Ms. Mahindaratne, that the witness first testifies A, and then in cross-examination, sometimes slightly changes or amends. If you would formulate it in such a way that we'll elicit from this witness what we want to elicit from him, and that we avoid any discussion as to -- if you just put the facts to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, Mr. Dzolic, the commander of the Knin military police company testified in these proceedings, and according to his testimony, without the mediation of the Military District command, missing equipment were recovered by the military police at the behest of General Cermak. So -- which you were not aware of?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So do you agree that based on that testimony that you were not fully apprised of the interaction between General Cermak and the military police with regard to tasks?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I wouldn't put it that way, since Mr. Cermak held daily meetings attended by representatives of all structures, especially in the early days after his arrival in Knin, the civilian authorities and partly military authorities, and I'm referring primarily to the civilian and military police, were briefed on daily events and developments at these meetings, which concerned the UN or any other issues. The military police could be informed of these matters at these daily meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo -- Mr. Dondo, the emphasis by Ms. Mahindaratne is that you were not fully -- as she said, fully apprised of the interaction. Now you explain to us that you were apprised of most of the interaction. Apparently the issue is that it was not a complete information. I think from your statement we've learned, and from your testimony, that there was interaction, but Ms. Mahindaratne gives you an example that are you not fully -- would you disagree with her that you were not fully - and I emphasise fully - apprised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can agree with that statement. I can agree that I wasn't familiar with the fact that she now mentioned. There was no order from Mr. Cermak to the military police to locate the vehicles. Rather, there were daily meetings at which Mr. Cermak informed both the civilian and military police of the requests he received from the UN to search for the vehicles, and this was a way in which they could have obtained that information. But I am not aware of the fact that he had found them, located them, and informed Mr. Cermak thereof. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, when you say -- you say that they may have this sort of way which they could have obtained that information, you're merely speculating, isn't it? You don't have a knowledge of this specific instance? You're merely speculating as to how the military police would have been informed of this instance. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can't remember all the things I remembered 15 years ago, but I'm sure that if Mr. Cermak had received a request from the UN which read that vehicles were missing, I am sure that he presented that letter at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, may I -- Mr. Dondo, may I just request that you do not speculate, and if you don't have a factual basis for an answer, if you do not know something as a fact, please say so. Now, you referred to the daily meetings that General Cermak held where the civilian police and the military police were present. Isn't that correct that liaison officers were not required to be present at these meetings mandatorily?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, as a result, isn't it correct that you were not present at all the meetings that General Cermak conducted with the civilian police and the military police in the mornings?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document number P390, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, you were shown this document by the Defence, and in fact, you have discussed this document. This is at paragraph 23 of D1696, and I'll just read that part of your statement to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Referring to this document you say: "I did not write the document titled 'Your letter of 10 August 1995 - freedom of movement,' dated 11 August 1995, marked P390, which you have shown me, but I knew that Mr. Cermak issued it. The letter was written in our office and we took it downstairs to Mr. Cermak's office to write it in the class and reference number. Mr. Cermak issued this letter because there was a great pressure from UNCRO for the freedom of movement, but the decision to allow UNCRO the full freedom of movement was made elsewhere because Mr. Cermak could not make this decision by himself." Now, whom did you refer to as the decision being made elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a decision could have been made only in the main command of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that would be? Are you referring to the Split Military District Command?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is it your position that General Cermak could not have issued authority or approval for freedom of movement without receiving an order to that effect from the Split Military District Command? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I want to show you -- in fact General Cermak himself discussed this document or at least this subject in your presence at the interview in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have P2526. And if could you go to English, on the English transcript, page 52; and that would be the Croatian version, page 62.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, this is what he says about his authority to issue -- on the subject of restriction of movement: "There were restrictions of movement but I don't why." This is halfway through the document. Then about four lines down in the same paragraph, then he says: "And then on the basis of the decision, this agreement between Sarinic and Akashi, I allowed freedom of movement to all the international organisations, all the international community, the Red Cross." Now at this stage, then he says a few more lines, there is an intervention from you. There is a discussion between you and General Cermak. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the full matters could be put to the witness, since we're reading it out. Line -- line 27, page 52.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could go through the intervention and if Mr. Kay would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I think it's -- if you're going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But see, you're inviting Ms. Mahindaratne to completely represent what is at stake here and what is relevant for the question. And I take it that you follow that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- invitation. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And after that you intervene at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could ask parties and Court to turn to on the additional translation, page 14; that is in the Croatian version, page 62. I'm sorry in the additional translation, page 52. I beg your pardon, page 14 which refers to the main transcript page 52.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then at that point you intervene, Mr. Dondo, and General Cermak asks you: "What are you saying?" You say, regarding the freedom of movement, you had to consult and ask Gotovina to grant the permission. That's what you advised Mr. Cermak at that point. And then General Cermak goes on to say: "When the international community asked for it, then we contacted the office and then it was allowed to all the organisations of the international community. They were allowed freedom of movement, not just in Knin, but in the whole sector. In the few days when there was restriction of movement in the operative zone, that was there when we got there. When we got there, and that was what the situation was, because I arrived on the 6th and I needed a couple of days to see what the situation was like."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then if could you move to page 54, Mr. Registrar, on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There, the second question, General Cermak is asked this question: "Because I wasn't there, I'm probably asking very stupid questions, but you just said that you called -- when you came to know about the restrictions you called Mr. Sarinic?" General Cermak answers: "Yes. "What exactly did Sarinic tell you? Cermak answers: "He told me that freedom of movement should be allowed to all the organisations, the UN and the Red Cross, in the whole area. "And why did I talk to him? Because he was the contact person for all the international organisations in the area." Two paragraphs down, the question is asked: "As a result of there discussion you had with Mr. Sarinic, what did you do?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move the text so that we can follow it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The answer: "I issued the order that all international organisations should have full freedom of movement in the whole area. And we informed General Gotovina about it."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And next page, that is page 55, Mr. Registrar, if could you move on to -- at the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The question is asked: "And now we come to the point where I'm confused. And I told you that there are things that I don't understand and I'm probably asking you very stupid questions. If you were under Gotovina, as you told us yesterday, how could you issue an order that they had full freedom of movement, if the initial order to keep them inside the compound was issued by a person who had power to issue such orders?" And General Cermak's response is: "Obviously this confuses you, but I immediately gave the order to all the international organisations to move freely around the area." At that stage, Mr. Dondo, you intervene again. This is on the same page as -- before page 14 of the additional translations. You say -- there's something unintelligible there: "... freedom of movement Gotovina banned. How could you grant the freedom if Gotovina had put a ban?" And General Cermak tells you: "No, about that ... What? I am listening." And whatever that -- the exchange goes on. So, Mr. Dondo, do you note that, at least in 1998 when General Cermak spoke to the OTP, his views about his authority and your views about what you're saying today about his authority are not the -- one and the same, isn't it? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree that he was presenting a situation differently to the way he does now. But my story now is the same as it was then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is General Cermak has moved, at least given different positions at different times with regard to his authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be translation issue or? Could you please repeat your question, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I didn't understand. Last question, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. As I understand your testimony, what you're saying is that Mr. Cermak has in fact changed his defences in the course of time. That's what you're telling?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he did, but the fact is, and you can see that in the documents here which show the same thing that I claim; namely, that Mr. Cermak could not have issued an order unless that was approved by the main command of the Operation Zone Split. And I know that when Mr. Cermak wrote the order on the freedom of movement, he said, Write it down, and I'll settle that with Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to Mr. Cermak's authority over the military police in Knin, Mr. Dondo, are you aware that General Cermak had instructed the military police in Knin to inform him of crimes committed by the military in General Cermak's area of responsibility? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, while we're on this document, if we could move back to page 49 of the English version. And that would be page 58 of the Croatian version. It's the paragraph that starts with "Okay." The question is asked from General Cermak: "Okay, I don't know if you are able to answer this question, but, if, for example, a Croatian soldier killed a civilian at the check-point in Knin, who would be the person who had the responsibility to take action [sic]? General Cermak responds: "That ever happened that a Croatian soldier killed a civilian anywhere, and not just in Knin, then it would be the military police that would take action because that would be just an ordinary criminal who wouldn't have any kind of special status. "Was the military police ordered or instructed to inform you about such incidents, if they happened? "Yes. I asked the military police to tell me what had happened, what happened so that I could tell the international community and organisations." Now, Mr. Dondo, does that also indicate to you that you were obviously not aware of the orders that General Cermak issued to the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, again, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At least with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the statement says, "I asked the military police." Your question is not referring -- it's referring to this being an example of not being aware of orders. Let's -- if it comes to requests, asking, ordering, where there is apparently disagreements between the parties how to understand what is put on paper, what is said, why not use the rather neutral term which does not affect your position that if the paper says it's an order, that you consider that to be an order, and, at the same time, does not affect the position of the Defence, which says you have to understand what is written down in the context of the powers to that person. Because that's the issue not for the first time. So, if we would use the other term that Mr. Cermak sought vehicles to be returned, et cetera, then we take a neutral term and then you can further ask him further detail about a piece of paper or what was said at a meeting, et cetera. But here, where Mr. Cermak said, "I asked," and then to say to the witness, Isn't this a clear example that he ordered, that is not assisting the Chamber. It's clear that he sought to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, do you -- does that this reflect, or do you agree with me that, based on what I just read to you, that you were not aware of specific instances of interaction between General Cermak and the military police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that I was not aware of every specific communication between General Cermak and the military police, but I can also confirm that I was present at the meeting where it was said, both to the civilian police and the military police, especially the civilian police, who, after the liberation of that territory had taken over control, that every crime that occurs in that area must be reported to him, because he will be fielding a lot of questions from the UN, and he must be ready to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Finally on this issue, Mr. Dondo, now, there are a number of documents that have -- that you have seen which has been shown to you by the Defence, that we went through today, and there are a number of documents in the evidence base, whereby General Cermak, on the face of the document it says that he orders the civilian police and the military police, and your testimony is that he, although the documents contain the term "order," that did he not have the authority to issue orders to the military police and civilian police. Now, is it then your position that General Cermak was issuing orders on a false premise, pretending to exercise an authority he did not have? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. From the interpreter, I hear the word "false," untrue premise, and that's the word that occurred yesterday in our debate, which is probably why it lasted so long. Mr. Cermak neither lied nor gave false statements. When he arrived in Knin as commander of the Military District -- as garrison commander, he signed orders as garrison commander Knin -- of Knin and issued orders on that basis. When he realised that these orders did not have enough power to attain their goal, he realised they were pointless. And in verbal communications with the civilian authorities of Knin, with the civilian police, with the military police and all the other agencies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo. Mr. Dondo, could you please focus your answer on the question that was put to you. That when Mr. Cermak issued what was said on paper to be an order, whether he issued these orders falsely; that is, that he suggested or presented to have an authority which did he not have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, yesterday when I asked you if you had acted as an intermediary between General Cermak and the civilian police and the military police, and I in fact specifically asked you if you had conveyed instructions from General Cermak to either -- either to the civilian police or the military police, you responded in the negative, and this is, for the record, at transcript page number 22482. Now, if you did not convey any instructions from General Cermak to the civilian police or the military police, or if did you not, by your own testimony, act as an intermediary between General Cermak and these two authorities, how would you know what kind of interaction took place between them, in order to assert that General Cermak did not have any authority over those two forces? Because, by your own testimony, you did not convey any instructions from General Cermak to either of these two forces.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cermak, as garrison commander, had a certain weight and an obligation to accomplish his mission, and faced with UN questions, he forwarded these questions to agencies that were supposed to answer them, that means the civilian, the military, and the special police. When he received their answers, he would forward them to us, either in writing or verbally, and we forwarded them to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if you would allow me to formulate one or two follow-up questions on my last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, you said Mr. Cermak did not issue orders falsely; that is, that he presented or suggested to have an authority which he did not have. Did Mr. Cermak, when he signed these documents which contained the text "I order," or "it is ordered," did he know that he no authority to issue this piece of paper by the name of "order"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not know, because when we came to Knin, there was quite a mess, I would say, in various inter-relations and relations among various commands, which I cannot go into, and orders appeared only in the beginning until this misunderstanding was resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you consider to be the beginning? Until what date? Three days, five days, ten days, a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me to speculate now. But I would say the first ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I didn't ask you to speculate, as a matter of fact, but you expressed that you maybe not be very precise but your recollection now is that it would have been approximately ten days. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware that issuing orders was beyond the authority of Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since he signed his name and his title, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the -- the garrison commander and you, in your function, as a matter of fact, you didn't know what the authority of Mr. Cermak was, and you just did what you considered to be useful for achieving the goals for which he was sent to Knin. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The latter. We did everything with best intentions, trying to achieve positive goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But with a lack of knowledge of where the authority ended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, possibly. I asked you whether you had knowledge or not, not ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Now, how did you know that Mr. Cermak had no knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did I know that Mr. Cermak didn't have information? Information about what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That he did not have knowledge as to whether it was within his authority to sign documents on which it says, "I order this," or "I order that"? How did you know that he had no knowledge what the limits of his authority were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that, that he had no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, one of the previous answers to one of my question, you said that he had no knowledge, isn't it? I asked you specifically about that. I said, Did Mr. Cermak know. I asked you: "Did Mr. Cermak, when he signed these documents, which contained the text "I order," or "it is ordered," did he know that he had no authority to issue this piece of paper by the name of order?" And then you said he did not know. Because when we came to Knin there was quite a mess, and then you started a lot of explanations. But your answer was that did he not know. Now my question is: How do you know that he did not know the limits of his authority? And now you say, I do not know; whereas, in one of your previous answers, you said Mr. Cermak did not know, suggesting that you knew about his knowledge of where the limits of his authority were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have to speculate again. I suppose that he, as a general who was dispatched to Knin, and was appointed and immediately had to leave, probably wasn't fully apprised of what his actual powers were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is pure speculation. You are speculating on the reasons why he would not know. But your answer is that you do not know whether he knew or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the earlier explanation where the witness was headed off from giving his answer right at the start of all of this, I think the witness was attempting to explain there the basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give me a line and a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can go back up to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that when he started about the mess upon arrival in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I am aware of what you're referring to, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, I put it to you that you do not know exactly as to what authority General Cermak had with the civilian police or the military police, and your testimony on this matter is all based on speculation. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm making -- I'm putting to you -- I'm making a proposition. You could answer as you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, this is the way to put a question to a witness in cross-examination. Ms. Mahindaratne puts to you that you had no knowledge, that it's pure speculation, and you can comment on what is put to you, whether you agree, whether you not agree, why you agree, why you do not agree. You may comment on this proposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, could you please repeat your assertion again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I put it to you that you do not know exactly what General Cermak's authority was over the military police and the civilian police in the Knin area, and your testimony, on that subject, is based on your speculation, mere speculation. That is my proposition to you. If you agree with me, you could say you agree with me; if not, you can say you disagree.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. There is speculation, of course, since I'm not familiar with all the facts. However, being privy to the events in Knin, I can say that he was familiar with the work of the military and civilian police, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That wasn't my question and let me just put one more point to you on this. In your 2005 statement to the OTP, at paragraph 10, this is what you say about this matter: "Mr. Cermak did not give us any specific tasks, but as we already had a role as liaison officers, we assumed that it would be the same. Mr. Cermak did not tell us what his role was to be and we were not told that we were to be subordinate to him. Our understanding that we still worked for the MOD but were supporting Mr. Cermak." Now, according to your own testimony, Mr. Dondo, General Cermak never discussed his role with you, and your -- therefore, I put it to you again, that your assertions made here about General Cermak's authority over the civilian police and the military police are based on speculation.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assertions about his powers over the civilian and military police are, indeed, based on speculation alone. Yes, I can assert that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just have a few more questions to you, Mr. Dondo. Yesterday you testified regarding the level of interpreters, the UN interpreters, and you stated that you could recall specific instances when, in fact, you had to request the replacement of some of those UN interpreters because the level of their -- the interpretation was poor. Now, can you tell us any specific instance when you made such a request from the UN, to replace interpreters?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two such instances. One involved a meeting with General Forand, where, and I can't name any names because I don't recall them, a girl was interpreting who made mistakes on three occasions, and we had to correct misinterpretation so that, ultimately, we asked that the interpreter be replaced because the terms she used changed the meanings of the sentences uttered. The second instance involved a meeting concerning the departure of a convoy, where individuals from the Croatian ministry were present. The interpretation was also poor, and we asked that one of the best interpreters present at the camp at the time show up. He was a young man who excelled at interpretation. He interpreted fluently and clearly. I can give you one or two more examples of the same type which involved minor meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the girl you referred to as having made -- where you had asked that she be replaced, if you go into private session, are you able to provide the name of that interpreter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was that request made to General Forand?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The request was stated at the meeting with General Forand, yes. General Cermak was there as well. Since we always had two interpreters on our side, precisely for the fact that we observed irregularities in interpretation, one of the two interpreters followed the interpretation of the other side to intervene where necessary, especially where it came to the various UN rules. So one of them basically dealt with the UN rules, the UN agreements and made sure that everything was interpreted correctly, and the other one followed the interpretation by the interpreter on the side of General Forand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, how do you assess your own fluency of the language English? Are you fluent?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak English well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I asked you that question because it has been suggested here in court, in fact by the Defence, that even your level of fluency in English was not sufficient. And this is at transcript reference 1166 to 1168. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sufficient for what, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It was said it is not sufficient to understand the conversations and interpret adequately. This is at reference 1166 to 1168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1166, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It might not be the exact words, Mr. President, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I'll check whether the ... Could you give me because in the early -- in e-court we have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, it isn't true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One -- well, if you give us time first to verify what was exactly said. Do you have a date for it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's the testimony of EJ Flynn, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The first day or -- no, most likely then the later days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me -- if I'm given a minute I could get that for you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I will find it. You said 1166.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 1166 going to 1168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me. Please proceed, meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The witness has already responded, Mr. President. I will -- shall I move on to the next area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'd -- not only to understand the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, I would like not only to understand the answer that something is not true, but also to know exactly what the question referred to. If you would ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have it anywhere in writing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, let me just -- if would you give me some time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, you are described in a piece of evidence as not being fluent in English at the time. Ms. Mahindaratne, that is what you referred to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- when you asked Mr. Dondo whether he agreed, and he said that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you answered -- yes, you said it is not true. If you have any further questions, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President I just have two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure which period of time this refers to, but it is certainly not true. I do not speak perfectly - I don't believe every Englishman does - but I do speak it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The reference, Mr. Dondo, was to 1995, the period, August up until November 1995, which is the subject matter of this indictment. However, you have responded to my question. Just one -- the last two questions from me, Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have P988, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now while that document is being brought up, you were in fact shown this document -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to page 7 of the English version, and in the Croatian version, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dondo, you were questioned about a statement you had made here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could focus on -- just --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see the title "Mass Grave in Knin Cemetery." There it is reported as follows: "The mission arrived at the Knin cemetery at 1530, accompanied by Cermak's liaison officer, Karolj Dondo, and an unidentified colonel described as an information officer. The cemetery is located on a dead-end street on the far north end of Knin." And then there is some description. Then you -- the last four lines from the bottom of that paragraph: "Mission members speculated that the military authorities wanted to give the impression that technical procedures had been used while burying the bodies, particularly since the liaison officer stated that the whole procedure had been done in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." Then the paragraph numbered 4.4: "The mission asked the liaison officer, Karolj Dondo, whether the ICRC had cooperated in the identification and burial of the bodies. He replied that the ICRC had participated in all phases of the process. "Upon return to Vienna on 21 August, the mission contacted the ICRC in Zagreb to verify the statement made by Karolj Dondo. A spokesperson for the ICRC in Zagreb denied categorically the claim that the ICRC had participated in any identification and burial of bodies in the Knin cemetery." So, Mr. Dondo, you had in fact made a false statement to these international monitors about the manner in which bodies were buried in the Knin cemetery. And in fact in explanation, when you were confronted with that fact by the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, in paragraph 33 of D1695, this is what you go on to say: "I have been asked about a Helsinki Committee report which states that I accompanied them to the Knin cemetery on or about 18 August. The report states that I said the burials were being done in conjunction with the ICRC but that the ICRC later denied any such involvement. It is possible that because I saw how well things were arranged at the cemetery, I simply made the assumption that the ICRC had been involved." So, Mr. Dondo, now, based on an assumption, you did not -- when you met these Helsinki Committee persons you did not tell them that you were simply assuming, but you have asserted that as a fact which proved to be completely incorrect. Now, once you got back from the office -- got back to the office, did you ever find out or at least make inquiries as to whether your assumption was accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I -- just one piece of clarity on this assumption because we seem to have merged to whether or not these bodies were buried in conformity with the Geneva Conventions or comments to the ICRC, because, of course, they're two different concepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it that Ms. Mahindaratne was focussing on the involvement of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, so you were asked -- you were asked what you stated for a fact; that is, that the ICRC was involved in all stages, which, as you then said, was an assumption, whether you ever verified the accuracy of this assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I verified it with the colonel who was in charge of information affairs, and he confirmed that it was accurate. I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When did you verify this?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the time in the cemetery when you made that statement to the Helsinki Committee representatives, you were only making assumption; is that correct? You didn't know, you didn't verify from any party as to whether the ICRC had participated in the burial process or not.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colonel for information and I discussed the matter on our way to the cemetery, where it had been stated that we actually assumed that this was the case, but neither of the two could be sure. That's why I presented it as my opinion, which I was not sure of, and then, subsequently, verified it with the colonel who confirmed it. I think it was after the first inquiry as to whether this was true or not. I verified the information with the colonel; I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it right, though, at the time when you made the statement, you made an assertion that the ICRC had participated and what is reported here is the whole procedure had been done -- I'm sorry. The ICRC had cooperated in the identification and burial of the bodies. He replied that the ICRC had participated in all phases of processes. Now you had -- you have stated that as a fact and in fact there was a witness here in court who testified about this matter. So my question to you is: Why did you make a statement to an international organisation, representatives of international organisation, based on -- on mere assumption?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because I thought that it was true and accurate. I believed that that was the case at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Dondo. I have no further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. I have one or two follow-up questions. Had you been at that cemetery before, Mr. Dondo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was it that struck you as so well done on the cemetery which made you believe that the ICRC would have been involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the graves were prepared in an orderly fashion and properly labelled. This was one of the many reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And some of the others, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, the colonel's assertion that the -- they had participated in the exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the reason to discuss it with the colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason was that until that morning I hadn't known I was to go to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But why to discuss this specific subject of ICRC being involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed, in general terms, what had happened and the bodies, how they were buried, and -- because it was said that it was a mass grave, and we claimed it wasn't. We claimed that all the bodies were buried in individual graves properly, that every grave was marked, and the international community - that is, the representative of the ICRC - was present during burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the colonel tell you how he knew all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was his position such that he would have first-hand knowledge of these kind of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this colonel was in charge of information, and I thought he was supposed to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say someone who is charged with information would know everything, or what is your perception of what an officer for information is usually doing? What's his main task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, in matters like this, he was supposed to know whether the victims had been buried and whether the procedure had been fully observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. My question is: Informations officer, is that someone who gathers information what happens within his own organisation, or is it someone who gathers information about what the opposite party is doing? What was his exact position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not his job to gather information about what the other side was doing. His job was officer for -- I can't remember the military title. Political activity within the army, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did he tell you that supervising funerals or burials was within his tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, dealing with matters, I hope, in order, you were asked questions about the interview that took place at the offices of Mr. Cermak in March of 1998, when the OTP interviewed him, and you were present. And do you recollect that you were asked questions about what you said during the interview and the fact of your presence there?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, did anyone from the Office of the Prosecution conducting the interview object to you being present?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did anyone object to the fact that you and Mr. Cermak may have discussed matters during the interview?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And your purpose for going along to the interview on that day in 1998 was what? Why were you there?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended that meeting to also serve as an interpreter, if so required. I mean, if Mr. Cermak asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked questions about the drafting of orders and the office procedures that were used in the garrison, and I think you'll remember looking at one or two, when asked questions by the Prosecution, and I want to ask you about those procedures now. Firstly, when you worked with Mr. Cermak, did he have any knowledge of the system of issuing orders in the military?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you worked before with any officers, in relation to their work and the need to draft orders at the request of the officer?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to compare Mr. Cermak's knowledge with those procedures, as compared to the knowledge of other officers you have worked with?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question. I don't think this arises from cross-examination, as to -- I have not gone into this witness's other experience. That doesn't even arise from any one of the statements. There is no testimony before the Trial Chamber as to this witness's experiences with other officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having consulted with my colleagues, the objection is denied. At the same time, Mr. Kay, the witness, in answer to one of your previous question, said that he didn't know what Mr. Cermak's knowledge was of the system of orders. Now you are asking him more or less to compare what he knew with others, and the Chamber considers it's appropriate that you first and then further explore what this witness knows about the knowledge of Mr. Cermak before you start comparing that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- that's what I was trying to do. I'm sorry if I was doing it clumsily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then because -- if he had no knowledge, it, certainly compared to others, then, of course, depends on what others know, but it couldn't be more. It could be the same or less. But it was not clear from your question whether you considered still to be some knowledge there, whereas, the witness said that he didn't know about -- let me just check exactly what the witness said. I'm focussing on -- let me just check. Yes, I'm referring to page 36, line 19, and the question in the two lines before that. Any knowledge. The witness apparently doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I will deal with this in a different -- different way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- which may assist the Court. And for this series of questions, if we go to the transcript, page 20, line 25 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were asked many questions on this subject about the authority of Mr. Cermak, what he knew, what his knowledge was, whether he knew what his knowledge was, whether you knew what his knowledge was. And during some answers to His Honour Judge Orie, a question was asked: Did Mr. Cermak, when he signed this documents which contained the text "I order," or "it is ordered," did he know that he had no authority to issue this piece of paper by the name of "order." And the answer that you partly gave was: "He did not know because when we came to Knin, there was quite a mess, I would say, in various inter-relations and relations among various commands, which I cannot go into, and orders appeared only in the beginning until this misunderstanding was resolved." So could you elaborate and explain what you were saying there?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that things that occurred at first in Knin were directed by the UN and other international organisations, primarily towards Mr. Cermak, particularly in view of the tasks that Mr. Cermak presented to us, saying that one of his tasks was to establish good communication and good relations with the United Nations. Our desire was to do our best to resolve the problems that occurred in the beginning, and, so, his requests that he received, be it regarding stolen vehicles or restrictions on movement, which occurred mainly in the beginning, were turned into orders, that they were formulated as such mainly in our office, in the belief that Mr. Cermak, in view of his position, was able to issue orders. In his daily duties, doing his job day to day, Mr. Cermak did not pay attention to the form of writings but the contents. He signed them and sent them to the relevant person or agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the -- what in fact happened. Were you able to see whether he was able to achieve those goals that he tried to achieve by issuing those documents?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, to the extent we were able to see things and get information, all his attempts and efforts were unsuccessful. And aside from that example that the Prosecutor cited that I'm not familiar with, I am not aware of any case where a positive result obtained after his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, in your original text as well, which you -- or the text which we see here where your answer to Judge Orie was, The misunderstanding was resolved, are you able to explain by what you meant in that phrase, in answer to Judge Orie's question?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give me the context?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll read out what you said again to remind you. "He did not know, because when we came to Knin, there was quite a mess, I would say, in various inter-relations and relations among various commands, which I cannot go into. And orders appeared only in the beginning, until this misunderstanding was resolved." And it's that's phrase "misunderstanding was resolved" that I'm asking you if you can explain further to the Court?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All can I say is that Mr. Cermak realised that his orders were pointless and that he could not issue them as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when in that answer as well you refer to, "There was quite a mess." "He did not know because when we came to Knin, there was quite a mess, I would say ..." Could you explain what you meant by that and how that is relevant to this issue?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is relevant insofar as Mr. Cermak himself did not know in the beginning whom to approach regarding certain problems that occurred in Knin at that time. The government, or the ministry, or the garrison command, the command of Sector South, or someone else entirely. That was at least the feeling I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you say that that was a -- a feeling. Is that based upon the facts that you witnessed and what you experienced at the time?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. Since I attended many meetings, I know that Mr. Cermak, General Cermak, would call up the ministry one day. The next day he would talk to Gotovina. The next day he would address Mr. Jarnjak. So there was no particular consistency to this chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in making those contacts and taking those steps, what was Mr. Cermak trying to do? Are you able to explain that?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually these contacts were made after meetings with the UN, when he was trying to deal with problems that had been presented to him at the meeting. As I said at the outset, these problems concerned mainly restrictions on the movement of UN forces, who wished to move outside the designated areas, and did so; and when they did so, they would be stopped by the Croatian Army, after which they would complain. In parallel, there were complaints about arson and other incidents also addressed to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just taking up what you said about the last matter, in relation to this, what was he attempting to do, in fact? And by that, I mean when you referred to the arson.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to arson incidents, he couldn't do much, except find out where these incidents had happened and inform the civilian police and ask for a report, whether this was, indeed, arson, as opposed to accidental fire, so that he could transmit the information to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning, now, to another subject. You were asked many questions concerning the events that took place in relation to the matter at Grubori, and you were referred to a UNTV interview that took place on the 26th of August. And a particular passage was put to you. I'll read it out from the transcript, first of all, before we go to the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And my learned friend asked this question: "Now based on your own findings, consequent to your visit to Grubori in the evening of the 26th of August, do you agree with me that Generals -- General Cermak's statement or interview given to UNTV crew in the morning of the 26th of August where he says that already civilian authorities had been to Grubori and had helped the people, is an inaccurate statement?" And you replied: "I do agree?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the words within the interview itself, which we can call up as Exhibit P504.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And on Exhibit P504, if we can turn to page 2 of the English document to look at the text there, we can see in the second paragraph, if we go to the third line, which this issue concerns: The Croatian civilian authorities have reached the village and taken care of the people, organised humanitarian aid for them and all other assistance required, so the people remained in their houses. And then if we go to the next Cermak answer again on this issue: The civilian police and authorities were in the village yesterday. I'm not aware whether the village was visited by someone this morning. I see no need why the police should go there today again. Now, were you aware at the time that on the 25th of August, the UN and internationals groups had scheduled a meeting in Plavno of the local population, and that is why they were up in that area at the time?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know whether Mr. Pasic and Mr. Romanic were due to go to Plavno on the 25th of August to that area?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'll ask no further questions about that. Were you aware of what the UN people who reported to you on the 25th of August, why they had been in the area and had come across this incident at Grubori?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN visited all the villages in the area at the time, in order to inform the people and collect all the people who were willing to leave the area for Serbia. I presume that that was one of the reasons why they were present in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know of any other functions or -- or tasks or jobs that they were doing, other than that collecting matter you were refer to? Did you know if they were doing any other jobs?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the jobs of the UN?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know -- you've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- to them going to the area, visiting the village. Did you know what else they were doing, or is that the full extent of your knowledge on the matter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, to the best of my knowledge, they toured villages and compiled lists of inhabitants present there. That was the extent of my knowledge at the time. They also had a bus of their own where they boarded the individuals who were willing to leave right away and transported them to Knin. We personally saw the bus out in the field when we were in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the report made to you by -- you describe an Italian lady, I believe, on the 25th of August, when you were informed that something had happened at Grubori and there was fire. You were asked if you had reported it to the civil police. Do you know if the UN people had reported it themselves to the civil police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they had, but I know that I told them to do so, to report that to the civilian police, in view of the fact that it was a criminal offence which falls within the competence of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you expected them then to go to the civil police themselves that day, to report the matter?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging from their reaction, I had, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were asked questions about the words concerning Operation Storm that were written in the Knin police log-book after your report to them of what happened in Grubori. Was Operation Storm still continuing at that time, or had it finished?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Storm had finished a while ago, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Dondo, I have a question related with your statement given by Defence, and I mention specifically paragraph 20. In this paragraph, you mentioned that you also participated in inspections of helicopters -- of UN helicopters, and as far as I understood, "We told Mr. Cermak that it would be a good idea if we, the liaison officers, supervise the inspection of the helicopters." My question is who -- who handed over these inspections?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr. Cermak that the initiative came from. It was our office that suggested the initiative to Mr. Cermak, given that, at the time, many Serb refugees were in the area, and among them, there were criminals who had not yet surrendered to the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our idea was that the situation had be to kept under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I'd like to interrupt you. I'm asking you who executed this -- this order or who actually carried out these inspections? Which body, military police, civil police?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I'm asking this particularly because I wanted to confront your statement with Dzolic transcript. Dzolic was chief of -- of -- of Knin Military Police Company. And in -- -- his statement was given on 17th September 2008, and then specifically referring on transcript pages 901 -- 9132, when I'm ask a question to him: Did military police participate in this such operations? And he -- he denied completely, saying that military police never carried out such inspections. My question is: Who tells it true?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: You mention here that 15 -- from 10 to 15 flights were inspected, as far as I understood. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And who -- who provide to you -- to you people from military police who ensures this inspection really? And how this inspection was carried out? Which tasks was prepared for this inspection especially?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows. The UN liaison officer would inform us of the helicopter's flight a day earlier and would give us the time of the helicopter's takeoff. On the same day, we would draft a written request, addressed to the military police headquarters in the Senjak barracks, unless I'm mistaken, where it would be handed over to the duty officer. On the following day, they would provide us with a military policeman who would come with us to conduct the inspection of the helicopter, since we as liaison officers were not authorised to carry out any sort of inspection or supervision. So it was a -- a procedure that had many -- that this had been -- taken place on many occasions. I think that the United Nations can easily confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And who drafted this written request and signed?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Liaison officers. After having received information from the UN, a liaison officer would draft a request for an escort of the helicopter, and that would be delivered to the duty officer of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will have just one question of the witness. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dondo, yesterday when Madam Prosecutor asked you about the report that you compiled on the 26th, following your visit to Grubori - and for everyone's reference this is page 63, line 20 of the yesterday's transcript - she asked you if you had observed any weapons in the area, and your answer was in the negative. Then the Prosecutor asked you whether you had seen any sort of weapons anywhere in the village and your answer again -- and your answer was that you didn't remember. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you during your visit to Grubori tour the entire village, go through every house and yard, or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KAROLJ DONDO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in fact where the entire misunderstanding lay between me and Madam Prosecutor, which resulted in a debate. When I went to Grubori, I went there as an observer, as a liaison officer, and not as an expert who would analyse the way in which the fighting took place there and the events that transpired there. I took note of what I observed at first glance, since there were only three -- two of us there, and since I knew that there had transpired a terrible incident there with grave consequences, you can imagine that to a certain extent we were afraid and unable to concentrate on individual details that could perhaps be found in different places in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
